easy.heading: A Gentle Morning Stretch
easy.body:
Today's easy puzzle was a lovely way to wake up the brain. I started by looking at the very top left where we had a sum region for cells 0,0 and 0,1 that needed to total 3. At the same time, I noticed a sum constraint of 6 for the cells 1,0 and 2,0. It felt like a little logic loop! I eventually figured out that placing the 2,2 domino vertically in the first column at 0,0 and 1,0 was the key. This meant cell 0,0 was a 2, making its neighbor 0,1 a 1 to hit that sum of 3.

From there, things really started to click. Since cell 1,0 was also a 2 from our 2,2 domino, cell 2,0 had to be a 4 to satisfy the sum of 6. This led me to place the 4,4 domino horizontally across 2,0 and 2,1. The final piece of the puzzle was the greater than constraint at the bottom. With cell 2,1 being a 4, cell 2,2 had to be a 5 to make the sum greater than 8. That worked out perfectly with the 0,5 domino fitting right into the last vertical slot.

medium.heading: Chasing the Chain Reaction
medium.body:
The medium puzzle felt like a series of falling dominoes, literally! I spotted a single cell region at 1,3 that had a target sum of 3, which is basically a free gift. That 3 had to be part of the 3,4 domino, which meant cell 0,3 was a 4. Once I had that 4, the sum region for 0,2 and 0,3 had to hit 8, so cell 0,2 also had to be a 4. It is so satisfying when one number just gives you the next one like that.

The trickiest part was managing the equal constraints near the bottom. I had to make sure the values at 3,0 and 3,1 matched, which then had to match the values in the 2,3, 3,2, and 3,3 cluster. By the time I got to the 5,2 and 6,2 dominoes, the board was getting pretty crowded. I had to be careful not to mix up the 6,0 and 6,2 dominoes, but once I realized cell 2,0 had to be a 0 to make the sum of 1 with its neighbor, the whole bottom row fell into place.

hard.heading: The Equals Sign Extravaganza
hard.body:
Wow, this hard grid was quite the journey! The sheer size was a bit much at first, but I found my footing by looking for the most restrictive spots. The single 3s at 0,0 and 0,6 were great starting points. I knew the domino at 0,0 and 1,0 had to involve a 3, and the same went for the one at 0,6 and 1,6. But the real breakthrough came from the massive equals regions. There was one chain where cells 3,3, 4,2, 4,3, 5,3, and 6,3 all had to be identical, which felt like a massive hint.

I spent a good chunk of time stuck in the middle near the 1,4 and 2,4 area. There was a sum of 11 for cells 3,4 and 4,4 that really limited my options. I realized I had to save my high value dominoes like the 5,5 and 6,3 for those high sum areas. Once I placed the 2,4 and 3,4 domino, the equals chain finally made sense and let me fill in five cells all at once. It was a long solve, but seeing all those equal values line up across the board was super rewarding.

explanation.tips: Try to find single cell regions first because they are essentially free numbers. After that, look for regions with very high or very low sums, like 11 or 2, because there are only a few dominoes that can actually reach those totals. If you are stuck, keep a physical list of the dominoes you have left so you can see which ones are the right shape and value for your remaining gaps.
explanation.learned:
Today I learned just how powerful the equals regions are for connecting different parts of the grid. In the hard puzzle, the equals constraints acted like a bridge that carried a single value from the middle of the board all the way down to the bottom. It makes the puzzle feel less like a series of small math problems and more like one big interconnected web.

I also noticed that the greater than constraints are often easier than they look. Instead of worrying about all the possibilities, you can usually narrow it down to just one or two options based on which high value dominoes, like 5s or 6s, are still available on your list. It is all about the process of elimination!

faqs.question: What are the basic rules for the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You must place a set of dominoes onto the grid so that every cell is covered. Each domino can only be used once. The pips on the dominoes must satisfy the constraints in each colored region, such as sums, equal values, or greater than comparisons.

faqs.question: How do equals regions work in Pips?
faqs.answer: An equals region means that every single cell inside that colored area must have the same number of pips. If you figure out the value of one cell in an equals region, you can immediately fill in all the others in that same region.

faqs.question: Can dominoes be placed diagonally in Pips?
faqs.answer: No, dominoes can only be placed either horizontally or vertically to cover two adjacent cells. They cannot be placed diagonally, and they cannot overlap each other.

faqs.question: What should I do if I get stuck on a hard Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: Start by double-checking your remaining dominoes. Often, you might have used a domino in one spot that is actually required for a high-value sum elsewhere. Also, look for empty cells that only have one possible neighbor left to form a pair.

faqs.question: Are the dominoes the same for every Pips puzzle level?
faqs.answer: No, each level has its own unique set of dominoes. The easy puzzle usually uses a small set with lower pip counts, while the hard puzzle uses a much larger set often going up to 6 pips per side.
